prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identified a compact, general mechanism: collateral constraints tie borrowing capacity to asset prices, so small shocks are amplified and propagated. The mechanism is conceptual rather than only applied, and it became a standard building block in macro-finance, quantitative macro and policy models, including post-2008 analysis. It is nearly three decades old, so its durability can be judged on a long record. The originating contribution is clean and sits with two people. That is the attribution property I value most under common criteria, and the three-name limit does not force arbitrary choices as it does for B035, B024 or B003. The candidate also has the broadest first-place and top-three support in the openings, but I treat that only as a signal that colleagues from different fields independently reached similar scientific judgments about influence and attribution, not as merit in itself.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and narrowness. The financial-accelerator strand (Gertler, Gilchrist, with Bernanke outside the credited list) is a parallel contribution, and several colleagues think the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises already covers part of this territory. A two-person award built on one seminal paper and its extensions may also under-credit the empirical and quantitative strand. Direct empirical validation of the amplification mechanism is mixed and more indirect than the theory's influence suggests. If the committee concludes that the 2022 prize leaves little marginal room, this candidate would weaken considerably.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B040 only seventh and flags possible overlap with the 2022 prize on banking and financial crisis research. He also asks whether the committee wants to credit the theory alone or the financial-accelerator line as well.
responses.response: The overlap concern is real and I do not dismiss it. I think it is a question of subject matter, not of the discovery. The 2022 recognition concerned banks, bank runs and the role of financial intermediation in crises. Kiyotaki-Moore is about the macroeconomic propagation of collateral constraints through asset prices and the dynamic interaction of credit limits and asset values. These are related but distinct contributions. I would keep the proposal to the two originators and not widen it to Gertler and Gilchrist. Widening it would deepen the overlap with a previously recognised literature and add attribution ambiguity. I would reconsider if the committee finds the mechanisms substantively indistinguishable.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 first and B040 fourth. He describes Kiyotaki-Moore as a conceptual advance with close to thirty years of influence, but notes that its empirical validation is more indirect than for other candidates and that the earlier Bernanke recognition complicates the framing.
responses.response: I agree on both points and put the empirical caveat among my own uncertainties. I would still separate influence from direct testability. The mechanism disciplined how a generation of macro models treat financial frictions and was used heavily in crisis analysis. I accept that B002 has stronger direct measurement, but its main results are about a decade old and its long-run causal interpretations are still being argued. That is a maturity difference, not a verdict against B002, and I keep it as a weighted consideration. On attribution I am less persuaded that the Bernanke link is a problem for a two-person award, because the originating claim is clean.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first, covering both the task-based framework and the China-shock evidence. She proposes Autor, Katz and Hanson, and notes that the trade-shock effects have been replicated but their size and persistence are still debated.
responses.response: I ranked B044 only eighth, and I now think that was somewhat low. The China-shock evidence is credible, well replicated and policy-relevant, and I take her point that the skill-bias and task literature has a longer record than the trade-shock papers alone. My remaining hesitation is structural. The task-based and trade-shock strands may be two separate contributions, and credit is split among Autor, Dorn, Hanson and Katz plus task-model authors outside the credited list. Her three-name configuration leaves out Dorn, who is a core author of the trade-shock papers. For that reason I keep B044 as an alternative, not my preferred part, and I would want the committee to settle which strand it is crediting before it settles on names.

responses.point: Hassler also ranks B040 first and keeps credit to the two originators. He argues that the financial-accelerator framework has been recognised in earlier prizes and that Gertler and Gilchrist belong to a distinct strand.
responses.response: I agree with the two-person attribution but would qualify the premise. I have not independently verified how much of the financial-accelerator strand the earlier prize actually credited. I would not rest the exclusion of Gertler and Gilchrist on prior recognition alone. The stronger argument is that their contribution is a distinct empirical and quantitative strand, and that adding names would blur the clean origin of the collateral-constraint mechanism. If that distinctness is contested, the committee should handle it on the merits as a separate question.

uncertainties: How much of the collateral-constraint and financial-accelerator territory the 2022 prize already covers, and whether that lowers the marginal case
Whether the committee prefers a broader macro-finance configuration that includes Gertler or Gilchrist for the empirical and quantitative strand
How much weight to give a mechanism whose direct empirical validation is mixed
Whether B044, B024 or B002 would, on further discussion, be judged to have a cleaner attribution or stronger maturity than B040
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the proposed laureates. The supplied profile lists no co-authorship, institutional or collaborative tie to Kiyotaki or Moore, and my research in market design, matching and auctions is a different field. I am an SSE affiliate alongside several committee colleagues, which is an institutional connection and not a tie to any candidate. For transparency, my first-ranked candidate lies outside my own field of expertise.
